On the other hand Mr. F.A. Mannan, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party contends that unless the amendment is allowed the plaintiff cannot get any effective decree in the suit for in the absence of the amendment the decree will be infructuous and that in such position the amendment is permissible under the provisions of Order 6 rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 5. The word 'real' contained in the provisions is quite significant. Every question that is raised by the parties are not the real questions of controversy in the suit. In a suit for specific performance of an alleged contract the real question that is to be determined and the real issue to be framed is whether there was a contract of sale between the parties and if the contract is proved then to decree the specific performance of such contract. The controversy as to whether the vendor had title when the contract for sale was made or whether the plaintiff would accuired title by having a kabala from the vendor by specific performance of contracts are not the real questions in controversy between the parties in a suit for specific performance of contract. These questions can only properly be raised and determined in a Title suit. 

 6. The amendment cannot be allowed under the provisions of Order 6 rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure to change the entire nature of the suit. As we have already observed. Order 6 rule 17 of C.P.C. is a provision for amendment of a pleading for a limited purpose i.e. the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties and in a suit for specific performance of contract the question relating to the title of the vendor and the title to be derived by the plaintiff opposite party on getting a decree are not the real question or issue or real controversy in the suit. 

 Mr. F.A. Mannan, the learned Advocate for the opposite party, contends that if the amendment is not allowed the decree to be got by him will be infructuous. This contention does not hold good. Even without the amendment the plaintiffs’ getting a decree is not obstructed for, if the plaintiff can prove the contract be will get the kabalas executed by the specific performance of the contract. Now whether he will acquire good title or not by that kabala will have to be got and settled by him in a properly framed title suit. The question of title between the plaintiff and other six persons who are not parties to the contract cannot be introduced or brought in a suit for specific performance of the contract. In a suit for specific performance of the contract the court has only to enforce the contract by having a kabala executed by the defendants. The court is not required to also declare or create title for the plaintiff the plaintiff will get only such title as his vendor had on the date of the contract. If the vendor had no title the plaintiff will not acquire any title. The declaration of title is not the proper subject and is not a matter of real controvery in a suit for specific performance of an alleged contract. M.R.S.C. Das, the learned Advocate for the petitioners further contended that the plaintiff had no cause of action against the persons whom be sought to add as party as they already purchased the suit land on the basis of an earlier contract and they had no concern with the subsequent contract that the plaintiffs claim to have made with the defendant petitioners. The contention of Mr. S.C. Das is of substance. According to the plaintiff's own case, he has no cause of action against these six persons who are sought to be added as party for the contract of sale was between the plaintiff opposite party and the petitioner defendants and the other six persons were not concerned with the said contract in any way. The plaintiff cannot therefore have any right of relief against those six persons.
